ERR_007.title: Gripper Malfunction

root_causes.diagnosis: Check pressure gauge - normal range is 80-120 PSI. Below 60 PSI indicates leak or compressor issue.
advanced_steps: Locate pressure gauge on gripper unit (usually on side panel)
Normal operating pressure: 80-120 PSI
If below 60 PSI: Check air compressor is running and set to correct PSI
Inspect all pneumatic lines for visible damage or disconnection
Listen for hissing sounds indicating air leaks
If leak found: Mark location, power off robot, call technician
If no leak but low pressure: Compressor may need service

root_causes.diagnosis: Inspect gripper pads for cracks, tears, smooth surfaces, or uneven wear. Pads should have texture/grip pattern.
advanced_steps: Power off robot for safety
Visually inspect both gripper pads (top and bottom)
Look for: cracks, tears, smooth/shiny surfaces, missing chunks
Check if texture/grip pattern is still visible
Measure pad thickness if possible (should be >5mm)
If pads look worn: This requires technician replacement
IMPORTANT: Pad replacement involves removing gripper assembly - DO NOT attempt without training

root_causes.diagnosis: Foreign object lodged in gripper mechanism or debris buildup.
advanced_steps: Power off robot completely
Manually try to move gripper (should have slight resistance but move)
If completely stuck: DO NOT force it - call technician
If moves but feels gritty: debris in tracks
Use flashlight to inspect gripper tracks and joints
Look for: cardboard pieces, plastic wrap, dust buildup, metal shavings
If debris visible: Use compressed air to blow out (wear safety glasses)
If object stuck: Carefully remove with tweezers/pliers
After cleaning: Test gripper in manual mode before resuming operations

root_causes.diagnosis: Faulty sensor, loose cable connection, or control board issue.
advanced_steps: Check gripper control cable connection at robot base
Look for loose, damaged, or corroded connectors
Firmly reseat all connectors (push until you hear click)
Check for bent pins in connectors
Inspect cable for cuts, pinches, or wear along entire length
If control panel shows error codes: Note down exact code numbers
Test gripper sensors: Use manual mode, wave hand near gripper
Sensors should detect objects 2-5cm away
If sensors don't respond or cable damaged: Call technician
This is an electrical issue requiring trained repair

common_operator_questions.question: Gripper looks fine but still won't work
common_operator_questions.answer: If visual inspection shows no issues, the problem is likely hydraulic pressure, electrical, or internal mechanical. Check the pressure gauge first (should be 80-120 PSI). If pressure is normal, this requires technician diagnosis with specialized tools to test sensors and control circuits.

common_operator_questions.question: How do I know if it's the pads or something else?
common_operator_questions.answer: If gripper opens and closes normally but can't hold items securely, it's usually the pads. If gripper won't move at all, or moves erratically, it's likely mechanical or electrical. If gripper moves but makes noise or feels rough, it's probably debris or worn bearings.

common_operator_questions.question: Can I replace the pads myself?
common_operator_questions.answer: No - gripper pad replacement requires: 1) Removing gripper assembly (involves disconnecting hydraulics and electrics), 2) Proper torque specifications for reassembly, 3) Pressure testing after installation, 4) Recalibration of grip force sensors. This MUST be done by a trained technician. Attempting DIY replacement can cause hydraulic leaks, electrical shorts, or safety hazards.

common_operator_questions.question: Gripper opens but won't close
common_operator_questions.answer: This is usually a one-way valve issue in the hydraulic system or a sensor stuck in 'open' position. First: Check if the pressure gauge drops when trying to close (indicates hydraulic leak). Second: Ensure nothing is blocking the close sensor. This typically requires technician service to replace the valve or sensor.

common_operator_questions.question: What if lubrication doesn't help?
common_operator_questions.answer: If lubrication doesn't improve movement, the issue is likely: 1) Internal bearing wear (requires replacement), 2) Bent or damaged gripper arms (requires realignment or replacement), or 3) Motor/actuator failure. All of these require technician service. Don't force the gripper or over-lubricate as this can cause damage.

safety_warnings: Always power off robot before inspecting gripper
Never put hands near gripper when robot is powered on
Hydraulic fluid under pressure - don't disconnect lines
Wear safety glasses when using compressed air
If gripper suddenly releases during operation, items may fall
escalation_criteria: Pressure below 60 PSI with no obvious cause
Basic troubleshooting steps don't resolve issue

ERR_013.title: Wheel Slippage Detected

root_causes.diagnosis: Check floor surface for water, oil, cleaning solution, or other liquids. Even small amounts can cause slippage.
advanced_steps: Stop robot immediately - continued slippage damages wheels
Inspect floor around robot for wet spots (3-5 meter radius)
Check if liquid is: water (clean), oil (slippery/greasy), or cleaning solution (sudsy)
For water: Use mop and dry thoroughly, set up fans if available
For oil/grease: Use degreaser and safety absorbent pads, then mop
For cleaning solution: May indicate scheduled cleaning in progress - coordinate with cleaning staff
Place 'Wet Floor' signs and caution tape around area
DO NOT move robot until floor is completely dry
Test dryness: Paper towel should come away completely dry when pressed to floor
After floor is dry: Inspect and clean robot wheels before resuming

root_causes.diagnosis: Inspect wheel treads for wear. New wheels have 3-4mm deep tread pattern. Worn wheels appear smooth or have <1mm tread depth.
advanced_steps: Power off robot and engage parking brake
Inspect each wheel (robot typically has 4 wheels)
Look for tread pattern depth - should be 3-4mm for new, minimum 1.5mm for safe operation
Check for: smooth/bald spots, uneven wear (one side more worn), cracks in rubber
Measure tread depth with ruler if possible
If tread depth below 1.5mm: Wheels need replacement - call technician
If uneven wear: May indicate alignment issue - requires technician diagnosis
Typical wheel life: 12-18 months depending on usage
DO NOT operate robot with worn wheels - safety hazard

root_causes.diagnosis: Plastic wrap, tape, cardboard, or other materials wrapped around wheels reducing traction.
advanced_steps: Power off robot completely
Visually inspect each wheel for debris
Common debris: plastic wrap, packing tape, labels, cardboard, wire, hair/fiber buildup
Manually rotate each wheel to see all sides
To remove debris:
- For plastic wrap/tape: Carefully cut and peel away (use safety knife)
- For stuck material: Scrape with plastic scraper (don't use metal - damages rubber)
- For fiber buildup: Use stiff brush to clean tread grooves
Clean each wheel thoroughly before moving to next one
After cleaning: Rotate wheels by hand - should spin freely without wobble
If wobble detected: Bearing issue - call technician

symptoms: Slippage only when carrying heavy loads
root_causes.diagnosis: Robot carrying more weight than designed capacity, causing wheel deformation and reduced traction.
advanced_steps: Check robot load capacity specification (usually 100-500 kg depending on model)
Weigh current payload if possible (use scale or check package weight labels)
If overloaded: Remove items until within capacity
Inspect wheels after overload event:
- Look for flat spots on wheels (indicates sustained overload damage)
- Check for bulging or deformed wheel sidewalls
- Test wheel firmness (should be firm, not soft/squishy)
If wheels damaged from overload: Requires replacement by technician
Prevent future: Train staff on weight limits, add warning labels, install load sensors
Consider splitting heavy loads across multiple trips

common_operator_questions.question: Floor looks dry but robot still slips
common_operator_questions.answer: The floor may have invisible residue (cleaning solution film, oil film, or concrete dust). Try these: 1) Wipe a small area with white cloth - if cloth shows dirt/residue, floor needs deeper cleaning. 2) Check if floor was recently cleaned (residue can remain 30-60 minutes). 3) Test different floor area - if no slippage elsewhere, it's definitely floor issue. 4) Consider floor material - some tiles become slippery when polished.

common_operator_questions.question: Only slips in certain areas of warehouse
common_operator_questions.answer: This indicates localized floor issue, not wheel problem. Causes: 1) That area may have different flooring material (tiles vs concrete). 2) Recent spill or cleaning in that zone. 3) Temperature/humidity difference causing condensation. 4) Floor sealant or wax applied unevenly. Solution: Mark problematic area, clean thoroughly, consider anti-slip treatment for that zone, or route robots around it.

common_operator_questions.question: How often should wheels be replaced?
common_operator_questions.answer: Typical wheel lifespan: 12-18 months with normal use. Factors affecting life: 1) Operating hours per day (more hours = faster wear). 2) Load weight (heavier loads = faster wear). 3) Floor surface (rough concrete wears faster than smooth). 4) Frequency of starts/stops (more wear). Check tread depth monthly - replace when below 1.5mm. Don't wait for complete failure.

common_operator_questions.question: Can I reduce robot speed to help with slippage?
common_operator_questions.answer: Yes, reducing speed helps temporarily but doesn't fix root cause. In robot settings, reduce max speed by 25-50%. This gives wheels more time to grip and reduces sudden acceleration forces. However: This is a TEMPORARY measure only. You must still identify and fix the actual problem (wet floor, worn wheels, etc.). Don't operate long-term at reduced speed as it affects productivity.

environmental_factors: Temperature: Below 5°C, rubber wheels lose flexibility and grip
Humidity: Above 80% can cause floor condensation
Floor type: Smooth epoxy floors more slippery than rough concrete
Recent floor maintenance: Wax, sealant, or polish affects traction
Traffic: High-traffic areas may have compacted dirt layer
safety_warnings: Robot may move unpredictably during slippage - keep personnel clear
Wet floors are slip hazard for humans too - mark area
Don't attempt to push or guide slipping robot manually
Overloaded robot with slippage can cause structural damage
escalation_criteria: Slippage continues after floor cleaned and dried
Wheels show flat spots or deformation
Unusual vibration or noise from wheels
Uneven wear pattern across wheels (indicates alignment issue)
